title: The Psychology of Collecting
instructions: For questions 1-8, read the text below and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.
passage:
Almost everyone, at some point in their life, has collected something, (1)___ it stamps, football cards or, in adulthood, vintage watches. Psychologists have long been curious (2)___ what drives this apparently universal urge.

One theory holds that collecting offers a sense of control (3)___ an otherwise unpredictable world: a complete set, however trivial the objects within it, is a small, achievable goal in a way that most of life is not. (4)___ said, the pleasure rarely lies in completion itself, since many collectors report feeling oddly deflated (5)___ they finally track down the one missing item.

(6)___ interesting is the social dimension collecting can acquire: swap meets, online forums and specialist fairs allow collectors to turn a private habit (7)___ a shared identity, often among people (8)___ would otherwise have little in common.

questions.explanation: 'Whether X, Y or Z' introduces a list of alternative examples without implying any real doubt or choice.
'Curious about' is the fixed adjective + preposition pattern used before a noun clause ('what drives...').
'A sense of control over something' is the standard collocation; 'over' expresses the idea of mastery or influence.
'That said' is a fixed concessive phrase meaning 'however', introducing a point that qualifies the previous sentence.
'Once' here functions as a time conjunction meaning 'as soon as', introducing the moment the missing item is found.
'Equally interesting is X' is an inverted structure (adjective phrase + verb + subject) used for emphasis, parallel to 'X is equally interesting'.
'Turn X into Y' is a fixed pattern meaning to transform one thing into another.
A relative pronoun referring to people is needed as the subject of 'would otherwise have little in common'.
